subtopic_detail: Severe cyclical irritability with full remission after menstruation in a woman seeking treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who says that for about a week before each period she becomes so irritable and tearful that she has twice considered resigning from her job. She describes feeling entirely herself again within two days of her period starting.

She has had this pattern for three years and it has worsened since stopping the combined oral contraceptive pill eighteen months ago. Her cycles are regular at 29 days. She sleeps and functions normally in the fortnight after menstruation, denies any low mood or anxiety at those times, and has never had a period of persistent low mood lasting more than two weeks. She uses condoms, does not smoke, and her thyroid function and full blood count taken by a colleague last month were normal. She has kept no record of her symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask her to complete a daily symptom rating record across two consecutive menstrual cycles
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles showing symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free interval after menstruation, because retrospective recall substantially overestimates cyclicity. Around forty percent of women referred with this history turn out on prospective rating to have a continuous mood disorder that worsens premenstrually, and that distinction changes treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at low dose taken continuously and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic treatment is genuinely effective here and can be given continuously or only in the luteal phase, but committing to it before the pattern is documented risks treating a continuous mood disorder as a cyclical one. Prospective rating costs two cycles and prevents that error. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Measure serum oestradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase to confirm a hormonal imbalance
options.rationale: Circulating oestradiol and progesterone concentrations are normal in this condition, which reflects an abnormal central response to ordinary cyclical hormone change rather than abnormal hormone levels. Measuring them generates uninterpretable results and false reassurance. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Refer for consideration of a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is a later step for severe disease that has not responded to first line measures, and it requires add back therapy and bone density monitoring. Escalating to it before the diagnosis is even established is disproportionate. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Refer for psychological therapy addressing the workplace stressors that appear to precipitate symptoms
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy has a genuine role in management, but framing the problem as workplace stress ignores a timing pattern that is tied to the cycle rather than to external events. Therapy is offered alongside a confirmed diagnosis, not instead of making one. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is defined by affective and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free interval in the follicular phase and demonstrable interference with function. Because retrospective reports of cyclicity are unreliable, the diagnosis formally requires prospective daily ratings across at least two consecutive cycles, most often using a validated instrument such as the daily record of severity of problems. The commonest alternative explanation is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying continuous mood or anxiety disorder, which prospective rating exposes immediately because symptoms never fully remit. Hormone concentrations are normal and measuring them does not assist. Once confirmed, effective options include serotonergic antidepressants given continuously or in the luteal phase only, combined hormonal contraception used in an extended regimen, cognitive behavioural therapy, and ovarian suppression for refractory disease.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily rating are required before the diagnosis is made
A symptom free follicular phase is the defining feature
Premenstrual exacerbation of a continuous mood disorder is the main alternative
Oestradiol and progesterone levels are normal and are not measured
Serotonergic agents work within days and may be given in the luteal phase alone
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants act within one to two days in this condition rather than the two to four weeks expected in major depression, which is why luteal phase only dosing from ovulation to the onset of menstruation is effective and is often preferred by women who dislike continuous medication.

subtopic_detail: Inability to tolerate vaginal penetration with involuntary muscle guarding on attempted examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse with her partner of two years. She says that whenever penetration is attempted her body tightens up and she feels she is being torn, and she has begun avoiding intimacy altogether.

She has never used tampons for the same reason. She describes her relationship as loving and reports no history of sexual assault or coercion. She has regular periods without pain and no vaginal discharge, itching or postcoital bleeding. On attempting examination she withdraws and her thighs adduct before you make contact with the introitus, and you are able to inspect the vulva only briefly. The visible vulval skin is normal with no fissuring, no pallor and no architectural change.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval skin with no fissures, pallor or architectural change, involuntary pelvic floor and thigh adductor contraction on approach to the introitus, internal examination not tolerated

options.text: Prescription of vaginal oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks to improve introital tissue elasticity
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary changes of oestrogen deficiency, which produce pale thin tissue and are seen after menopause or with prolonged lactation or ovarian suppression. This woman is cycling normally with normal appearing vulval skin. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation and pelvic floor down training
options.rationale: Involuntary pelvic floor contraction preventing penetration, with normal vulval skin and no other pain condition, is treated first with pelvic floor physiotherapy using graded exposure, dilator work and techniques to release rather than strengthen the muscle. This has the strongest evidence of any single intervention and works through the involuntary guarding that is the core of the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Prescription of topical lidocaine gel applied to the introitus for twenty minutes before intercourse
options.rationale: Topical anaesthesia targets a localised nociceptive trigger at the vestibule and is useful in provoked vestibulodynia, where touch to a specific point reproduces burning pain. It does not address involuntary muscle contraction and can be used as an adjunct rather than as the primary treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Examination under general anaesthesia to exclude an obstructing vaginal septum or other anomaly
options.rationale: Structural anomaly is worth considering but is unlikely with regular painless menstruation and no history of obstructed flow, and anaesthesia removes the very muscle response that defines the condition. It is reserved for cases where anatomy genuinely cannot be assessed after treatment has begun. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

options.text: Referral for botulinum toxin injection into the levator ani muscles under sedation as definitive therapy
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is a second line option for women who have not responded to physiotherapy and psychological treatment, and evidence remains limited with effects that wear off over months. Offering it first exposes her to an invasive procedure ahead of a conservative approach that usually succeeds. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual pain disorders)

explanation.summary: Persistent difficulty with vaginal penetration accompanied by marked involuntary tensing of the pelvic floor and adductors, and by fear or anxiety about penetration, is classified within genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder. Assessment must exclude dermatological causes such as lichen sclerosus, infection, and structural anomaly, and must ask sensitively about prior trauma without assuming it. The single most effective intervention is pelvic floor physiotherapy, which teaches awareness and voluntary release of the muscle, combines graded dilator exposure with relaxation, and is typically paired with psychosexual therapy and partner involvement. Topical anaesthetics, oestrogen and botulinum toxin all have narrower indications and are adjuncts or second line. Progress is measured by tolerance of graded insertion rather than by achievement of intercourse, which reduces the performance pressure that maintains the cycle.
key_points: Involuntary muscle guarding, not tissue pathology, is the core mechanism
Exclude lichen sclerosus, infection and structural anomaly before attributing to muscle
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded dilators is the highest yield first intervention
Psychosexual therapy and partner involvement improve outcomes and are offered alongside
Botulinum toxin and surgery are later options after conservative treatment fails
explanation.pearls: Set the treatment goal as comfortable tolerance of a graded dilator or a tampon rather than as intercourse, because making penetration the measure of success reinstates the anticipatory anxiety and reflex guarding that the physiotherapy programme is designed to unlearn.

subtopic_detail: Smooth cervical lesion found at screening in a woman reporting bleeding after intercourse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a routine cervical screening test on a 41 year old woman who mentions that she has bled a few times after intercourse over the past three months.

On speculum examination there is a smooth, bright red, pedunculated lesion about 12 mm long protruding from the cervical os on a narrow stalk. The surrounding ectocervix looks healthy with no ulceration, no friable irregular tissue and no induration on palpation. Her previous screening test two years ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Her periods are regular and she has no intermenstrual bleeding, no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. Her result returns today as negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated bright red cervical lesion 12 mm on a narrow stalk arising from the os, healthy surrounding ectocervix, no ulceration or induration, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not tender
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, previous test two years ago also negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to gynaecological oncology given that postcoital bleeding with a cervical lesion is present
options.rationale: Urgent oncology referral is driven by a hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix, contact bleeding from an abnormal looking surface, or a cervix that feels indurated on palpation. A smooth pedunculated lesion on a narrow stalk with a healthy surrounding cervix does not meet that threshold. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Cervical cancer)

options.text: Prescribe a course of doxycycline and metronidazole for presumed cervicitis and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antimicrobial treatment addresses infective cervicitis, which presents with mucopurulent discharge and a friable inflamed cervix rather than a discrete pedunculated lesion. Treating empirically leaves the visible lesion in place and the bleeding unexplained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Remove the lesion in clinic by twisting the stalk and send the tissue for histological examination
options.rationale: A benign appearing pedunculated cervical polyp causing postcoital bleeding is removed by avulsion of the stalk in the clinic, which both stops the bleeding and provides tissue. Histology is mandatory because a small proportion harbour unexpected pathology and because polypoid appearance alone cannot exclude it. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

options.text: Reassure her that a negative screening test excludes significant pathology and repeat testing in five years
options.rationale: A negative human papillomavirus result reduces the risk of squamous disease but does not investigate a visible cervical lesion or exclude adenocarcinoma, which is less reliably detected by screening. Any symptomatic or suspicious visible lesion is assessed on its own merits regardless of the screening result. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling before any attempt is made at removal
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding and at risk factors for endometrial pathology, and this woman has neither. Imaging is added when the polyp appears to arise from higher in the canal or when bleeding continues after removal. (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal uterine bleeding)

explanation.summary: Cervical polyps are common benign lesions arising from the endocervical canal or ectocervix and are a frequent cause of postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. The essential clinical task is to distinguish a benign pedunculated polyp with a healthy surrounding cervix from a malignant lesion, which typically appears as a hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix. A negative human papillomavirus screening result is reassuring for squamous disease but must never be used to dismiss a visible lesion or a symptom such as persistent postcoital bleeding, since adenocarcinoma arises higher in the canal and is less reliably captured. Symptomatic polyps are removed by avulsion of the stalk in the clinic, with the specimen sent for histology because a small minority contain unexpected pathology. Persistent bleeding after removal, or a polyp whose base cannot be seen, prompts imaging and hysteroscopic assessment for an endometrial origin.
key_points: Smooth pedunculated lesion with a healthy surrounding cervix suggests a benign polyp
A hard irregular friable or ulcerated cervix warrants urgent oncology referral
A negative human papillomavirus result never overrides a visible or symptomatic lesion
Avulsion in clinic treats the bleeding and provides tissue for histology
Bleeding persisting after removal prompts imaging and hysteroscopy for an endometrial source
explanation.pearls: Send every avulsed polyp for histology even when it looks unequivocally benign, because a small number contain endometrial or endocervical adenocarcinoma or high grade dysplasia, and discarding the specimen removes the only opportunity to detect a lesion whose visible appearance was reassuring.

subtopic_detail: Device stem palpable at the external os on routine check after insertion
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman six weeks after insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device. She reports cramping and irregular bleeding since insertion and says her partner can feel something hard during intercourse.

She has been using no other method of contraception since insertion and had unprotected intercourse four days ago. Her last menstrual period began nine days ago. On speculum examination the threads are visible but the firm white stem of the device is protruding about 1 cm through the external os. The uterus is anteverted, normal in size and non tender, with no cervical excitation and no adnexal tenderness. She is afebrile and there is no offensive discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Device stem visible protruding approximately 1 cm through the external os with threads present, uterus anteverted and non tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass or tenderness, no offensive discharge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to confirm the device position before deciding on any intervention
options.rationale: Ultrasound is used when threads are absent and the device cannot be seen, to distinguish complete expulsion from perforation or a high lying device. Here the stem is directly visible in the canal, so imaging adds delay without changing the plan. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Reassure her that irregular bleeding settles by six months and review the device position in three months
options.rationale: Unscheduled bleeding in the first six months is indeed expected and usually settles, but that counselling applies to a correctly positioned device. Leaving a displaced device in place exposes her to unintended pregnancy for three months. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Take endocervical swabs and treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease before removing the device
options.rationale: Pelvic infection is suggested by fever, pelvic tenderness, cervical excitation or offensive discharge, none of which are present. Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea remains reasonable on risk grounds but empirical treatment and delay are not warranted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Remove the device now, provide emergency contraception cover and arrange a replacement insertion
options.rationale: A device whose stem sits within the cervical canal is partially expelled and no longer provides reliable contraception, so it is removed rather than pushed back up, and a new device is inserted. Because she had unprotected intercourse four days ago while the device was already displaced, emergency contraception is required alongside the removal. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

options.text: Reposition the device upwards into the uterine fundus using an instrument under direct vision
options.rationale: Pushing a partially expelled device back through the internal os is not recommended because it damages the device and the endometrium and the expulsion usually recurs. The correct action is removal and reinsertion of a new device. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Intrauterine contraception)

explanation.summary: Expulsion of an intrauterine device occurs in roughly two to ten percent of users and is most likely in the first three months, with heavy menstrual bleeding, insertion immediately postpartum and a history of previous expulsion increasing the risk. Partial expulsion, where the stem lies within the cervical canal, removes contraceptive reliability even though threads remain visible, and it presents with cramping, unscheduled bleeding or a partner feeling the device. Management is removal and insertion of a new device rather than repositioning, since repositioning damages the device and expulsion recurs. Contraceptive cover must be considered because the device may have been displaced for some time, so emergency contraception is offered when there has been recent unprotected intercourse and a pregnancy test is performed. Ultrasound is reserved for missing threads, where the alternatives are complete expulsion, a high lying device or uterine perforation.
key_points: Partial expulsion means the device stem lies in the cervical canal and is no longer reliable
Expulsion risk is highest in the first three months after insertion
Remove and replace rather than reposition a partially expelled device
Consider emergency contraception because the device may have been displaced for days
Ultrasound is for absent threads, to separate expulsion from perforation or high position
explanation.pearls: The copper device is the more effective emergency contraceptive but is unsuitable in this situation, so if a new hormonal device is inserted at the same visit, cover the preceding episode of unprotected intercourse with oral ulipristal or levonorgestrel and remember that ulipristal reduces the effectiveness of a hormonal method started in the following five days.

subtopic_detail: Couple asking when to stop other contraception after male surgical sterilisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38 year old woman and her 41 year old partner for a joint appointment about contraception. He had a vasectomy eleven weeks ago and they want to know whether she can now have her hormonal implant removed.

He reports that the wound healed without incident and that he has ejaculated well over thirty times since the procedure. He has not yet provided any semen sample, saying the clinic gave him a form but he did not get around to it. They have three children and are certain their family is complete. She has tolerated the implant well and is keen to stop it as soon as it is safe to do so. Neither has any other medical history.

data_table.Examination: Well healed scrotal incisions, no haematoma, no tenderness, testes normal to palpation
data_table.Investigations: No post procedure semen analysis performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Advise that the implant can be removed now because more than twenty ejaculations have occurred
options.rationale: Ejaculation count was historically used as a proxy but is unreliable, since a proportion of men still have motile sperm after twenty or more ejaculations. The reason the analysis exists is precisely that this proxy fails in a minority. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Advise that the implant can be removed once sixteen weeks have elapsed from the date of the procedure
options.rationale: A fixed interval without testing does not establish clearance, because clearance depends on the individual rate at which residual sperm are cleared rather than on the calendar. Some men take considerably longer and a small number never clear. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Arrange scrotal ultrasound to confirm that the vas has been successfully divided on both sides
options.rationale: Imaging does not assess whether sperm are still present in the ejaculate and is used for suspected haematoma, abscess or chronic scrotal pain after the procedure. The functional question is answered by semen analysis alone. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

options.text: Remove the implant and advise condom use for a further three months as a precautionary measure
options.rationale: Substituting a highly effective long acting method for condoms increases typical use failure substantially during the very window when the outcome is still uncertain. The precaution should be maintaining the existing effective method rather than downgrading it. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception)

options.text: Continue the implant until a semen sample confirms clearance, and arrange that analysis now
options.rationale: Sterility is confirmed only by post procedure semen analysis, usually collected from around twelve weeks and after a sufficient number of ejaculations, because residual sperm persist in the distal vas for a variable period. Time elapsed and ejaculation count alone are not accepted as proof, so existing contraception continues until a clearance result is issued. (Source: RACGP: Vasectomy)

explanation.summary: Vasectomy does not produce immediate sterility because sperm persist in the vas deferens distal to the point of division, and clearance is confirmed only by post procedure semen analysis. Australian practice is to test from around twelve weeks after the procedure, and existing contraception is continued until a clearance result is issued. A result showing azoospermia confirms success, while persistent non motile sperm in low concentration may permit clearance at the operating surgeon's discretion, and persistent motile sperm indicates failure requiring repeat testing or a repeat procedure. Early recanalisation occurs in roughly one in two hundred to five hundred men and late recanalisation is rarer still, so couples are counselled that no method is absolutely permanent. Counselling before the procedure should also confirm that the decision is regarded as permanent, since reversal is expensive, not funded and has variable success.
key_points: Residual sperm in the distal vas mean sterility is not immediate
Semen analysis from around twelve weeks is the only accepted confirmation
Ejaculation count and elapsed time are unreliable proxies for clearance
Continue existing contraception until a clearance result is issued
Late recanalisation occurs rarely, so no method is presented as absolute
explanation.pearls: Persistent low concentrations of non motile sperm on repeat testing can be accepted as special clearance by the operating surgeon rather than triggering a second operation, but any motile sperm at three months means the procedure has failed and the couple must keep using contraception while a repeat is arranged.
